sycophant

SIK-uh-fant · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Sycophant is a person who flatters someone powerful in order to gain advantage.

Court records from the era are full of sycophants competing for the queen's smallest favor.

Worked Example

The king surrounded himself with sycophants who praised every decision, however foolish.

Praising every decision, however foolish, is exactly sycophant behavior.

Your Turn

Answer correctly to continue.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

flatterer: A flatterer is anyone who lays praise on too thick, for any reason — kindness, habit, nerves, or gain. A sycophant is a flatterer with a strategy: the target is always someone powerful, and the praise is always an investment meant to pay off.

toady: Toady and sycophant name the same self-serving flatterer, but a toady grovels: the fawning is open, crude, bowing-and-scraping low. Sycophant is the more formal, classical term, and it covers even the smooth, dignified flatterer whose praise never looks like begging.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

doubter: a person who questions and doubts claims

Where it sits · how self-serving the flattery is — admirer → sycophant → leech

admirer vs. sycophant: An admirer sincerely respects someone; a sycophant flatters specifically to gain personal advantage, sincere or not.

leech vs. sycophant: A leech is a step beyond even a sycophant in self-interest: a sycophant at least pays for favor in praise and attention, while a leech simply attaches itself to a powerful person and drains money, gifts, and influence, giving nothing back.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — syco

root — syco: fig (Greek (sykon))

root — phant

root — phant: to show (Greek (phainein))

Put it together

Put it together: Sycophant comes from Greek sykon ('fig') + phainein ('to show') -- literally 'one who shows the fig,' from an ancient Athenian phrase whose exact original meaning is debated, possibly tied to informing on illegal fig exporters.

Use the root in a new word: emphasis

Use the root in a new word: emphasis: The same phainein root gives us the everyday word emphasis, literally 'a showing in' -- both words are built on that same idea of 'showing.'

Root Check

Word Choice

Sycophant is the more formal, classical term for a flatterer seeking personal advantage from someone powerful, distinct from "toady" (taught in this same unit), the more casual everyday word for the same role.
